name: Survivorship Bias
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Counting the Planes That Made It Back
lesson.summary: Survivorship bias, drawing conclusions only from the visible successes while the failures quietly disappear from view, distorts the public sense of how steadily quantum computing research is actually progressing.
lesson.body:
During the Second World War, military analysts studied bomber planes returning from combat missions, mapping where on the aircraft the bullet holes were most concentrated, with the reasonable-sounding plan of adding extra armor to those heavily damaged areas. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out that this reasoning was backwards. The planes being studied were the ones that survived and made it back. Planes hit in other locations, ones that did not show up as commonly damaged in the surviving sample, likely went down and never returned to be examined at all. The areas that looked undamaged on the surviving planes were, if anything, the most critical to reinforce, precisely because damage there tended to be fatal. This is now the canonical illustration of survivorship bias: drawing conclusions from a visible sample that has already been filtered by an earlier selection process, without accounting for what that filtering removed.

The structural problem generalizes well beyond aircraft. Whenever the data available to you has already passed through a filter that disproportionately removes failures, a naive reading of that visible data will overstate how well the underlying process is actually going, because the denominator, the full set of attempts including the ones that failed, is invisible.

Quantum computing coverage shows this pattern clearly. A new qubit count record, a headline-grabbing demonstration of so-called quantum advantage on a narrowly chosen benchmark task, or a well funded startup's product launch each receive substantial press attention, understandably, since they are genuinely notable events. Meanwhile, quietly discontinued corporate quantum computing programs, shut down startups, and research groups whose funding was reduced or redirected receive comparatively little coverage, because there is no natural news hook for an announcement that did not happen. Someone following only the visible headlines over several years would reasonably conclude that quantum computing is on a steady, uninterrupted march of progress, without ever seeing the full set of attempts that did not pan out.

None of this means the visible milestones are fabricated or unimportant, most are real technical achievements worth taking seriously on their own terms. The distortion is specifically in the inferred base rate: the field can look like it is succeeding more consistently than the complete picture, including the unreported setbacks, would actually support, in exactly the same way that the surviving bombers made certain parts of the plane look safer than they really were.

The practical corrective is to actively ask, whenever a quantum computing progress claim appears, what you are not seeing alongside it: which programs quietly shrank, which predictions from a few years ago quietly got walked back without an announcement, which companies pivoted away from quantum hardware. That question does not require dismissing the genuine milestones, it requires refusing to let the highlight reel stand in for the full record.
